newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.N. says Bosnia mass graves disturbed.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Bosnia mass graves disturbed.

text.p: Forensic experts working for the U.N. war crimes tribunal discovered that two mass grave sites in Bosnia had been tampered with before the start of their excavations, the U.N. said on Wednesday.
The revelation came as deteriorating weather conditions forced the tribunal's criminal investigatiors to suspend the grisly work of exhumation and identification until 1997.
U.N. spokesman Alexander Ivanko in Sarajevo said there was evidence Pilica, one of four mass grave sites under investigation, had been disturbed.
A tribunal spokesman in The Hague told Reuters a site at Lazete had also been tampered with.
"From what I understand a number of bodies and/or parts of bodies may have been removed before the tribunal team arrived in the area," Ivanko said of the Pilica site.
"All we can say is that the site has been tampered with in what seems to be in a pretty sloppy way."
The tribunal began exhumations in July and has been active at four grave sites -- Cerska, Nova Kasaba, Lazete and Pilica.
All of the graves were believed to contain the remains of victims killed after Serb forces overran the Moslem enclave of Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia in the summer of 1995.

Thousands of Moslems, mostly men and boys, are missing and presumed dead in the aftermath of the Serb onslaught. Surviving eyewitnesses have identified about a dozen mass grave locations associated with the fall of Srebrenica.
U.N. sources said investigators had recovered between 400 and 500 bodies from the four sites investigated to date.
They could not be more precise about the number because the remains were badly decomposed in many cases and parts of several skeletons might have been mixed together during recovery.
Former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and his army commander, General Ratko Mladic, were indicted by the U.N. tribunal for war crimes at Srebrenica. Both remain at large.

NATO-led peace forces deployed in Bosnia to help implement the provisions of the Dayton peace agreement have refused to provide fixed security at suspected mass grave sites despite widespread fears that valuable evidence might be destroyed.
Instead, NATO has relied on roving patrols and aerial surveillance to deter and detect tampering, with uncertain success.
Ivanko explained that, despite the end of exhumation operations for 1996, forensic experts would continue working out of the morgue in Kalesija, east of Tuzla.
U.N. scientists at the morgue examine recovered human remains to try to determine time and cause of death as part of the continuing criminal investigation into Bosnian war crimes.
Tribunal investigators on Tuesday handed over to Bosnian government authorities the skeletons, clothing and anthropological information on 33 bodies exhumed from Nova Kasaba in July.
U.N. sources said that only two of the bodies carried documentation which might lead to their final identification.
